extracted.intended_audience: Patent examiners in the U.S. Patent Examining Corps
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and workshop worksheets for formulating a subject-matter-eligibility (35 U.S.C. §101) rejection and for evaluating an applicant's response under the Mayo/Alice two-part framework. Focuses on what an Office action must say, what evidence/analysis is required, and how to assess applicant arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide clear explanation and sufficient notice
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why the claim is ineligible, which must be sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice of the reasons for ineligibility and enable the applicant to effectively respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action should explain why the claim is ineligible in a way that allows applicant to identify grounds and respond; worksheets and examples emphasize clarity and specificity as a threshold requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the judicial exception in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Has a judicial exception been identified? The Office action must identify the judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea) that the claim is allegedly directed to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worksheet asks examiners to mark whether a judicial exception is identified and to state 'The judicial exception is:' — examiners should explicitly name the exception (e.g., 'abstract idea of advancing funds based on future retirement payments').

rubrics_metrics.name: Point to specific claim words that recite the judicial exception and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the rejection point to words of the claim that recite (set forth or describe) the judicial exception? Is there an explanation of why those words are a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should cite particular claim language and provide reasoning (not mere conclusory labeling) explaining why those words correspond to the identified judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify additional elements beyond the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Are any additional elements identified? The rejection should list additional claim elements beyond the judicial exception (e.g., memory, processor, network interface, controller, kiosk components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the worksheet to list the additional elements and ensure they are expressly identified in the rejection before assessing their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze significance of additional elements individually
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the explanation address the significance of the additional elements individually? The Office action should analyze whether each additional element, by itself, provides 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must avoid conclusory statements that an element is 'generic' without explaining why; if asserting an element is routine/conventional, provide factual support or citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze significance of additional elements as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the explanation address the significance of the additional elements as a combination? Taken as a combination, do the elements amount to significantly more than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action should consider whether the elements together improve the functioning of a computer or effect a technical solution (vs. merely performing generic computer functions). The exemplary action warns that 'looking at the limitations as an ordered combination adds nothing that is not already present when looking at the elements taken individually' unless a meaningful improvement is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support findings of routine/well-understood/conventional with documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make conclusory statements that components are routine or conventional without evidence. If the rejection asserts that components perform well-understood, routine, and conventional activities, documentary evidence should be cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant example emphasizes that the examiner 'failed to provide any documentary evidence' and that mere conclusory statements are insufficient to establish a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Mayo/Alice two-part framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the two-part analysis for claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception; (2) if so, determine whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop assumes participants are familiar with the two-part analysis; the exemplary Office action demonstrates stepwise application (identify abstract idea, then evaluate additional elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address preemption concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim would 'preempt' all uses of the purported abstract idea; preemption is the concern driving the abstract-idea exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze whether the claims tie up the broad concept or leave alternative techniques open; applicant arguments may show alternative implementations (e.g., different methods of calculating benefit or different transfer mechanisms) to rebut preemption concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Machine-or-Transformation (M-or-T) test as a useful clue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Machine-or-Transformation test is a 'useful and important clue' for determining patent eligibility and should be considered where appropriate (e.g., whether the claim is tied to a particular machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant arguments may rely on M-or-T to show eligibility (e.g., claim recites a particular computer system integral to the invention); examiners should weigh this alongside Alice/Mayo analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether recited computer elements are merely generic or a claimed special-purpose machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess if the computer components recited at a high level of generality merely perform generic computer functions (and thus add nothing) or if the claim ties those components to particular programmed functions rendering a special-purpose machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplar notes that 'generic computer components recited as performing generic computer functions...amount to no more than implementing the abstract idea' but also acknowledges precedent (In re Alappat) that a programmed general-purpose computer can be a special-purpose computer; analysis must be specific to the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider secondary factors (commercial success/market evidence) when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success and other objective indicia (market acceptance) may be relevant in evaluating whether a claimed invention is merely an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant argued that significant commercial success is inconsistent with a claim being 'nothing more than an abstraction' and examiners should consider such evidence where provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: When evaluating applicant responses, track each argument and rate persuasiveness with explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a response-evaluation worksheet to record 'What is Applicant's Argument?' and mark whether it is persuasive or not persuasive, with an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section V provides a chart for tracking each applicant argument, whether persuasive, and an explanation — examiners should consider all amendments, arguments, and evidence when making the persuasiveness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a prima facie case of ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Before withdrawal is appropriate, examiner must make a prima facie case of unpatentability under §101 — this requires more than conclusory assertions; it requires evidence and clear reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant's responsive remarks emphasize that the examiner 'failed to establish a prima facie case' by not providing documentary evidence; the Office action should contain sufficient explanation and factual support to establish the prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether dependent claim limitations provide 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate dependent claim limitations (e.g., kiosk with interactive display, network connector, smart card dispenser) to determine whether they, alone or in combination with independent claim limitations, provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant argues that dependent elements describe a distributed computing environment producing a nonroutine action (ejection of a debit card) and that a new combination of known elements may be patentable even if constituents are known (Diamond v. Diehr). Examiners should analyze whether the combination produces a technical improvement or merely an extra-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the Office action links claimed features to the legal standards/case law
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection should explain how claim features relate to judicially-identified abstract ideas and cite relevant caselaw or guidance (e.g., Alice, Bilski, Mayo, Diehr, Alappat) where that linkage is informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exemplary rejection maps the concept to court-identified concepts (intermediate settlement, risk hedging) and discusses how those precedents inform the conclusion. Examiners should show the analogy and provide supporting explanation.
